narrative:
The model predicted an 80.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 also worked against you, though its influence was smaller. It sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore added a modest additional push toward predicting failure.

Other details such as your LSAT score of 31, upper-middle family income, Hispanic background, female gender, and plan to attend full-time played little or no role in the outcome. The system focused almost entirely on your school performance.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking key courses to raise your GPA, seeking academic support to move up in class rank, or strengthening other parts of your profile before reapplying. Many students successfully reapply after addressing these exact gaps.
